# Introduction to ggplot2

Before we get into unsupervised learning, we'll take some time to introduce plotting in R.

R has a tidyverse package called ggplot2. ggplot2 provides a domain-specific language for data visualisation. You build plots incrementally, starting with a simple plot object and adding features with a special addition (`+`) operator. Each addition returns a new plot object. Hence, the `+` operator allows you to compose plot instructions to build plots from simple building blocks.

Here's a simple example (we'll unpack it shortly):

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)
```

- The **gg** in ggplot2 stands for **Grammar of Graphics**.
- ggplot2 is based on Grammar of Graphics, a language proposed by Leland Wilkinson for describing statistical graphs:
    - Wilkinson, L. (2005), _The Grammar of Graphics_, 2nd ed., Springer.
- Useful Resource: [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/)

Plots are described as a stack of layers, with each layer describing one of the following attributes:

- **Data**: The dataset (rows = cases, columns = variables)
- **Aesthetics (aes)**: Visual properties mapped to data (x, y, colour, fill, size, shape, etc.)
- **Geoms**: Geometric objects that draw marks: points, lines, bars, boxplots, etc.
- **Stats**: Statistical transforms that summarise data before drawing: binning, smoothing, density estimation, counts, summaries
- **Scales**: Scales map data values to the visual values of an aesthetic. To change a mapping, add a new scale.
- **Coordinates**: How data space is mapped to the plotting plane: Cartesian, polar, map projections, flipped coordinates
- **Facets**: Facets divide a plot into subplots based on the values of one or more discrete variables.
- **Position**: Position adjustments determine how to arrange geoms that would otherwise occupy the same space.
- **Theme & Guides**: Non-data ink: fonts, grid lines, margins, legend placement; legends and colour bars

## Example Dataset

We'll introduce ggplot2 using R's built-in `mtcars` dataset, which relates car weight (`wt`) to miles per gallon (`mpg`), plus a few other features.

Here are the first few rows:

```{r}
head(mtcars)
```

Here's a minimal example of a scatter plot of `wt` vs `mpg` from the built-in `mtcars` dataset:

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
```

This short chunk does three things:

1. Declares that the `mtcars` dataset supplies the data.
2. Maps car weight to the x-axis and miles per gallon to the y-axis via the aesthetics function (which we'll see a lot of).
3. Adds a single geometry layer with `geom_point()` to draw the scatter plot.

Nothing else is specified, so every other plot component—scales, coordinates, guides, and theme—falls back to ggplot2's defaults.

## Adding Stats

The above plot was quite basic. We can enhance it by adding a grid and a smoothing line:

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "red") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.25)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(se = TRUE)
```

`geom_smooth()` adds a smoothed line to the plot, helping to visualise the trend in the data. The gray ribbon (below) shows a confidence interval around the smooth.

## Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics

If we add a colour aesthetic inside `aes()`, ggplot2 will map the colour to a variable in the dataset and create a legend:

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.25)
  )
```

_(注：此处原幻灯片代码中 `theme()` 块重复出现了两次，恢复时已去重)_

We can also use the point colour to represent another variable, such as horsepower (`hp`):

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = hp)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.25)
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C")
```

- `colour = hp` maps horsepower (a continuous variable) to color intensity
- `scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C")` uses the viridis color scale

## Facets: Small Multiples

Facets divide a plot into subplots based on the values of one or more discrete variables.

- `facet_wrap(~ cyl, nrow = 1)` creates separate panels for each cylinder count (4, 6, 8)
- `nrow = 1` arranges all panels in a single row
- Each panel shows the same x-y relationship but filtered to cars with that specific cylinder count
- This is powerful for comparing patterns across different subgroups

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.25)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~cyl, nrow = 1)
```

_(注：原 PDF 文本中提取为 `facet_wrap(-cyl)`，根据 R 语法和图片逻辑修正为 `~cyl`)_

## Complex Plot Example

Finally, here's a more complex example combining several of the elements we've discussed:

```{r}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency vs car weight",
    x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    colour = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.25),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8.5),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7.5)
  )
```
